title: The Riemann integral defined
objectives: Define the Riemann integral with upper and lower sums, and prove that continuous functions are integrable.

screens.title: Trap the area

screens.title: More pieces
screens.prose: A **partition** $P$ of $[a, b]$ is a finite list $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$. The **upper sum** $U(f, P)$ uses the supremum of $f$ on each piece, the **lower sum** $L(f, P)$ the infimum. Move $n$, the number of equal pieces.

hints.text: Set $n = 10$ and read both sums.

feedback.correct: Right. $U = 0.385$ and $L = 0.285$ at $n = 10$, a gap of 0.1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the slider to 10 and subtract the lower sum from the upper sum.

byKey.square: You squared the width. The gap is the width itself, 0.1.

explain.text: Each sliver has height $f(x_k) - f(x_{k-1})$ and width $\tfrac1n$. The heights telescope to $f(1) - f(0) = 1$, so $U - L = \tfrac1{10} = 0.1$.

screens.title: The gap in general
screens.prose: Summing squares gives, for $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$ with $n$ equal pieces, $$U_n = \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n^2}, \qquad L_n = \frac{(n-1)(2n-1)}{6n^2}.$$
screens.question: Simplify $U_n - L_n$.

hints.text: Expand both numerators.
The difference is $6n$; divide by $6n^2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the numerators first: the $2n^2$ and the 1 cancel.

byKey.two: You doubled the gap. The numerators differ by $6n$, not $12n$.
byKey.sq: You divided by $n$ once too often. $\tfrac{6n}{6n^2} = \tfrac1n$.
byKey.third: That is the area, which both sums approach. The question asks for their gap.

explain.text: The numerators differ by $(2n^2 + 3n + 1) - (2n^2 - 3n + 1) = 6n$. So $U_n - L_n = \tfrac{6n}{6n^2} = \tfrac1n$, as the slider showed. Both sums squeeze $\tfrac13$, since $U_n = \tfrac13 + \tfrac1{2n} + \tfrac1{6n^2}$ and $L_n = \tfrac13 - \tfrac1{2n} + \tfrac1{6n^2}$.

screens.title: Fine enough
screens.prose: Call a partition good enough when its sums are within 0.01 of each other. For equal pieces, the gap is $U_n - L_n = \tfrac1n$.

state.caption: $n = 20$: the gap is $\tfrac1{20} = 0.05$, still too wide.

screens.question: What is the smallest $n$ with $U_n - L_n < 0.01$?

hints.text: Solve $\tfrac1n < 0.01$.
That is $n > 100$.
$n = 100$ gives exactly 0.01, which is not below it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $\tfrac1n < 0.01$ for the first whole number $n$.

byKey.sqrt: You solved $\tfrac1{n^2} < 0.01$. The gap is $\tfrac1n$, not $\tfrac1{n^2}$.

explain.text: $\tfrac1n < 0.01$ means $n > 100$, so the first whole number is 101. For every $\varepsilon > 0$ some $n$ works, by Archimedes (l4). That is exactly the test for integrability.

screens.title: The Riemann integral
screens.prose: On a piece let $M_k = \sup f$ and $m_k = \inf f$. Then $$U(f, P) = \sum_k M_k\,\Delta x_k, \quad L(f, P) = \sum_k m_k\,\Delta x_k.$$ A bounded $f$ is **integrable** when $\inf_P U = \sup_P L$, and this value is $\int_a^b f$. Equivalently, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ some $P$ has $U - L < \varepsilon$.
screens.question: Add points to $P$, making a finer partition $Q$. What happens to the sums?

options.text: $L$ rises or stays, and $U$ falls or stays.
Both sums rise, since there are more rectangles.
options.why: You counted rectangles. More pieces are thinner, so the total width stays $b - a$.

options.text: Both sums become equal to the integral.
options.why: Extra points narrow the gap but rarely close it. For $x^2$ the gap is still $\tfrac1n$.

options.text: Either sum can move either way.
options.why: Splitting a piece replaces one supremum by two over smaller sets. Each is at most the old one, so $U$ cannot rise.

hints.text: Split one piece in two. Compare the old supremum with the two new ones.
A supremum over a smaller set is at most the supremum over the larger set.
So each new top is at most the old top, and each new bottom at least the old bottom.

feedback.correct: Right. Refining can only tighten the trap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how large a supremum over half a piece can be, compared with the whole piece.

explain.text: Split a piece at $t$. The supremum over each half is at most $M_k$, so the two new rectangles fit under the old one. So $L(f, P) \le L(f, Q) \le U(f, Q) \le U(f, P)$ for every refinement $Q$.

screens.title: A function with no area
screens.prose: The Dirichlet function on $[0, 1]$ is $f(x) = 1$ for rational $x$ and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise. It is bounded. By density (l4), every piece of every partition holds both rationals and irrationals.

screens.title: One delta for every point
screens.prose: $f$ is **uniformly continuous** on $A$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $|x - y| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x) - f(y)| < \varepsilon$, for all $x, y \in A$ at once. For $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$, $$|x^2 - y^2| = |x - y|\,|x + y| \le 2|x - y|.$$
screens.question: What is the largest $\delta$ this bound gives, as a formula in $\varepsilon$?

hints.text: We need $2|x - y| < \varepsilon$.
That holds when $|x - y| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$.
So $\delta = \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, the same for every $x$ and $y$.

feedback.correct: Right. $\delta = \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, and it does not depend on where we are.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $2|x - y| < \varepsilon$ for $|x - y|$.

byKey.times: You multiplied by 2. The window must shrink to beat the factor 2: divide.
byKey.same: With $\delta = \varepsilon$ the bound gives only $|x^2 - y^2| < 2\varepsilon$.

explain.text: $|x - y| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ gives $|x^2 - y^2| \le 2|x - y| < \varepsilon$. One $\delta$ serves every point, because $|x + y| \le 2$ on $[0, 1]$. On all of $\mathbb{R}$ the factor $|x + y|$ is unbounded, and no single $\delta$ works.

screens.title: Continuous on a closed interval
screens.prose: Theorem: a continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$ is uniformly continuous. The proof is by contradiction, with Bolzano-Weierstrass (l9). Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose not. Then some $\varepsilon_0 > 0$ beats every $\delta = \tfrac1n$: there are $x_n, y_n \in [a, b]$ with $|x_n - y_n| < \tfrac1n$ and $|f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \ge \varepsilon_0$.
$(x_n)$ is bounded, so a subsequence $x_{n_k} \to c$ by Bolzano-Weierstrass, and $c \in [a, b]$ because the interval is closed.
By the triangle inequality, $|y_{n_k} - c| \le |y_{n_k} - x_{n_k}| + |x_{n_k} - c|$, which is below $\tfrac1{n_k} + |x_{n_k} - c|$. So $y_{n_k} \to c$ too.
$f$ is continuous at $c$, so $f(x_{n_k}) \to f(c)$ and $f(y_{n_k}) \to f(c)$.
So $|f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k})| \to 0$, against $|f(x_{n_k}) - f(y_{n_k})| \ge \varepsilon_0$ for every $k$. Contradiction. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: That $\delta$ came from $|x + y| \le 2$, a fact about $x^2$. A general $f$ has no such formula, so the proof argues by contradiction.

lines.text: By Bolzano-Weierstrass, $(x_n)$ itself converges to some $c$.
lines.why: Bolzano-Weierstrass gives a convergent subsequence, not convergence of the whole sequence.

hints.text: Start by negating uniform continuity.
The negation: one $\varepsilon_0$ beats every $\delta = \tfrac1n$, at some pair of points.
Extract a subsequence of the $x_n$, show the partners $y_{n_k}$ follow it, then use continuity at the limit.

feedback.correct: Right. Negate, extract, drag the partner along, then let continuity clash with $\varepsilon_0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The order is: negate, extract a subsequence, show $y_{n_k}$ has the same limit, use continuity, contradict.

byKey.d1: You used the formula from $x^2$. A general $f$ gives no formula; the proof works by contradiction instead.
byKey.d2: You let the whole sequence converge. Only a subsequence is promised.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Closed and bounded enter through Bolzano-Weierstrass and $c \in [a, b]$. Continuity at the one point $c$ then controls both partner sequences. On $(0, 1]$ the argument fails for $\tfrac1x$, since the limit $c = 0$ is outside.

screens.title: Continuous functions are integrable
screens.prose: Let $f$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and let $\varepsilon > 0$. We build a partition $P$ with $U(f, P) - L(f, P) < \varepsilon$. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: By uniform continuity, choose $\delta > 0$ such that $|x - y| < \delta$ implies $|f(x) - f(y)| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{b - a}$.
Take any partition $P$ whose pieces all have width less than $\delta$.
On each piece $f$ attains $M_k$ and $m_k$ (l17) at two points less than $\delta$ apart, so $M_k - m_k < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{b - a}$.
So $U(f, P) - L(f, P)$ equals $\sum_k (M_k - m_k)\,\Delta x_k$, which is less than $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{b - a}\sum_k \Delta x_k = \varepsilon$. $\blacksquare$
Choose a $\delta_k$ at each point $x_k$, from continuity there.
lines.why: Pointwise choices can shrink towards 0 across the interval, so no one mesh need work. Uniform continuity gives one $\delta$ for every piece.

hints.text: First fix one $\delta$ for the whole interval.
A mesh below $\delta$ puts the top and bottom of each piece within $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{b - a}$.
Sum $(M_k - m_k)\,\Delta x_k$; the widths add to $b - a$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix $\delta$, choose the mesh, bound each piece, then add.

byKey.d1: You chose $\delta$ point by point. Those can shrink towards 0; the proof needs one $\delta$ for all pieces.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: For $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$ with $\varepsilon = 0.01$, this route takes $\delta = 0.005$, so $n \ge 201$ equal pieces. The exact gap $\tfrac1n$ needs only $n = 101$. A proof needs a bound that works, not the best one.

screens.title: Upper and lower sums as code
screens.prose: Write `upper_lower(f, a, b, n, increasing)` for a monotone $f$ on $[a, b]$ with $n$ equal pieces. Return the pair $(U, L)$. When `increasing` is true the tops are at the right ends; otherwise at the left ends. With `Fraction` inputs the answer is exact.

params.title: Expected
lines: >>> upper_lower(lambda x: x*x, Fraction(0), Fraction(1), 4, True)

screens.question: Complete the function.

widget.starter:

    """(U, L) for a monotone f on [a, b] with n equal pieces."""
    ...
widget.solution:
from fractions import Fraction

def upper_lower(f, a, b, n, increasing):
    """(U, L) for a monotone f on [a, b] with n equal pieces."""
    w = (b - a) / n
    xs = [a + k * w for k in range(n + 1)]
    left = sum(f(x) for x in xs[:-1]) * w
    right = sum(f(x) for x in xs[1:]) * w
    if increasing:          # tops at the right ends
        return (right, left)
    return (left, right)    # falling: tops at the left ends

isinstance(upper_lower(lambda x: x*x, Fraction(0), Fraction(1), 3, True)[0], Fraction)

screens.title: Averaging a price path
screens.prose: An Asian option pays on the average price over a year, $\int_0^1 S_t\,dt$. Desks approximate it with 250 daily fixings. Take a path rising steadily from £100 to £110 over the year.

state.caption: Ten fixings drawn; the desk uses 250.

screens.question: With 250 fixings, by how much do the upper and lower sums differ?

hints.text: The path rises, so each top sits at the right end of its day.
As for $x^2$, the slivers stack to the whole rise, £10, over a width of $\tfrac1{250}$.
$U - L = 10 \times \tfrac1{250}$.

byKey.rise: You gave the whole rise, £10. The slivers each have width $\tfrac1{250}$.
byKey.square: You divided by 250 twice. The rise stacks into one column of width $\tfrac1{250}$.

explain.text: For a rising path the gap telescopes to $(S_1 - S_0) \times \tfrac1n = 10 \times \tfrac1{250} = \text{£}0.04$. The true average lies inside that band. Integrability is why finer monitoring converges to one price for every continuous path.

ideas: A partition cuts $[a, b]$ into pieces. $U(f, P)$ uses the supremum on each piece and $L(f, P)$ the infimum. For bounded $f$, refining never lowers $L$ or raises $U$.
$f$ is integrable when $\inf U = \sup L$: for each $\varepsilon$ some $P$ has $U - L < \varepsilon$. For $x^2$ on $[0, 1]$, $U_n - L_n = \tfrac1n$; the Dirichlet function keeps $U = 1$, $L = 0$.
Continuous on $[a, b]$ means uniformly continuous, by Bolzano-Weierstrass. A mesh below $\delta$ then makes $U - L < \varepsilon$.

formula.name: Integrability criterion
formula.note: Then $\int_a^b f = \inf_P U(f, P) = \sup_P L(f, P)$.

summary.trap: The upper sum takes each piece's top wherever it sits. That is the right end for a rising $f$, the left end for a falling one.

quiz.prose: $P$ and $Q$ are any two partitions of $[a, b]$, and $f$ is bounded.
quiz.question: Which inequality always holds?

options.text: $U(f, P) \le U(f, Q)$ when $P$ has fewer points
options.why: Fewer points usually means a larger $U$. And without $P \subseteq Q$, the two need not compare at all.

options.text: $L(f, P) = L(f, Q)$ when both have $n$ pieces
options.why: Pieces of different sizes give different sums. Only refinement gives a comparison.
You flipped the trap. Tops sit above bottoms, so upper sums are the larger.

feedback.correct: Right. Every lower sum lies below every upper sum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare both with the common refinement $P \cup Q$.

explain.text: Let $R = P \cup Q$, which refines both. Then $L(f, P) \le L(f, R) \le U(f, R) \le U(f, Q)$. So $\sup L \le \inf U$ for every bounded $f$, and integrable means they meet.
